raw_response.blind_rationale: Blind reading of Mutono et al. (2022) confirms that excluding S483 from SWiM Families A, B, and C (`none_nonfit`) is fully justified, and further flags the study as borderline `E03` for PI scope review under narrow Criterion 2. Specifically: (1) Criterion 4 is clearly satisfied (`yes_household_or_service_access`), as the primary outcome is monthly domestic piped water consumption per capita (and water sufficiency >= 1500 L/capita/month) across 2,380 residential utility billing itineraries in Nairobi from 2008 to 2018, supplemented by weekly supply hours under rationing (Table 3). (2) However, under narrow Criterion 2 (`borderline_governance_or_proxy`), the primary multivariable negative binomial mixed-effects model (Table 4, PDF p. 10) tests NCWSC's four-tier residential classification (High-income R1, Middle-income R2, Middle/low-income R3 vs. Low-income R4), built-settlement age (GHS-Built land-cover conversion era), their interaction, and itinerary population count. Although R1–R4 originated in municipal land-use master plans (1973/1979/2014) and NCWSC's 1985 water distribution plan—with R4 encompassing low-income housing and unauthorised shanty dwellings, and NCWSC organizing weekly water rationing schedules by R1–R4 (Table 3)—the authors explicitly operationalize and validate R1–R4 via KSCBS household cross-tabulations (Table 1A, n = 1,137) as a proxy for neighbourhood socio-economic status because census small-area SES statistics were unavailable. Neither land tenure security (Table 1A: 85% in R1 vs. 48% in R4), water rationing hours (Table 3: descriptively higher in R4 at 78 h/week vs. 59 h/week in R1, opposite to the consumption gradient), nor kiosk tariff non-enforcement (Section 2.1.3) is statistically tested as an independent rule exposure predicting water consumption or sufficiency. (3) Consequently, pooling Table 4's residential income-tier Rate Ratios (RR = 5.78 for high-income vs. low-income areas) into Family A (tenure/recognition) or Family C (utility regulation/administrative capacity) would conflate socio-economic wealth, housing density, in-house plumbing, and private tank storage with a legal or regulatory rule effect. Two internal reporting discrepancies in the source paper are also noted: first, Table 4 models continuous/count monthly per capita water consumption (Rate Ratios = 5.78, 3.80, 1.65), whereas the Abstract and Section 3.3.1 text misdescribe those exact Rate Ratios and CIs as the relative likelihood of achieving the binary >= 1500 L/capita/month sufficiency threshold; second, in Table 4, 'Built up before 1975' prints RR = 0.54 with a narrow CI of 0.53–0.56 alongside an inconsistent p-value of 0.425.

raw_response.headline_estimate_summary: Multivariable negative binomial linear mixed-effects model (year as random effect; adjusting for residential category, built-settlement age, residential category x built-settlement age interaction, and annual itinerary population count; no SEs reported) of monthly per capita domestic piped water consumption across N = 2,380 residential itineraries in Nairobi (2008–2018; Table 4, PDF p. 10 / journal p. 9): vs. Low-income areas (R4, n = 252, reference), Rate Ratio (RR) = 5.78 (95% CI: 5.34–6.25, p < 0.001) in High-income areas (R1, n = 534), RR = 3.80 (95% CI: 3.52–4.10, p < 0.001) in Middle-income areas (R2, n = 772), and RR = 1.65 (95% CI: 1.53–1.79, p < 0.001) in Middle/low-income areas (R3, n = 822) [note: Abstract and p. 9 text round these RRs to 6x, 4x, and 2x and misstate them as likelihood of >= 1500 L/capita/month water sufficiency]. Built-settlement age (vs. built up after 2014, n = 218): before 1975 RR = 0.54 (CI: 0.53–0.56, printed p = 0.425), 1975–1990 RR = 0.62 (CI: 0.60–0.65, p < 0.001), 1990–2000 RR = 0.87 (CI: 0.85–0.89, p < 0.001), 2000–2014 RR = 0.96 (CI: 0.94–0.99, p < 0.001); Population count RR = 0.85 (CI: 0.71–0.93, p < 0.001); plus age-by-residential-category interaction RRs in Table 4. Descriptive statistics (PDF pp. 8–10, Tables 3 & 1A): mean monthly consumption = 13,087 L (R1, 7% <1500 L/cap/mo), 6,240 L (R2, 12% insufficient), 1,697 L (R3, 36% insufficient), and 827 L (R4, 60% insufficient); average weekly supply under rationing (Oct 2016–Dec 2018) = 59 h (R1), 50 h (R2), 65 h (R3), and 78 h (R4); non-revenue water (Nov 2016–May 2018) = 29% (3.5 billion L/month).
raw_response.study_design_and_sample: Spatio-temporal ecological panel analysis (2008–2018 monthly utility billing records, plus 1985 vs. 2018 land-use/network comparison, Oct 2016–Dec 2018 rationing schedules, and Nov 2016–May 2018 reservoir metering) in Nairobi, Kenya. Unit of analysis: Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company (NCWSC) geographical billing 'itineraries' (average population ~700 people). Analytic sample: N = 2,380 residential itineraries (out of 2,538 georeferenced itineraries after excluding 554 unlocated itineraries and 158 non-residential itineraries from ~3,000 total itineraries). Supplemental cross-sectional validation sample: N = 1,137 households across 7 Nairobi sublocations from the 2012–2013 Kenya State of the Cities Baseline Survey (KSCBS; Table 1A: R1 n = 60, R2 n = 170, R3 n = 161, R4 n = 746).
